title: How Much Do Solar Panels Cost in 2026? Real Prices by State & City
excerpt: The average 6kW solar system costs $14,000–$20,000 before incentives in 2026, dropping to $9,800–$14,000 after the 30% federal tax credit. Costs vary significantly by state, city, and installer.
content:
Average Solar Panel Cost in 2026

The national average cost for a residential solar installation in 2026 is approximately $2.75–$3.50 per watt before incentives. For the most common system sizes: 4kW system: $11,000–$14,000. 6kW system: $16,500–$21,000. 8kW system: $22,000–$28,000. 10kW system: $27,500–$35,000. After the 30% federal Investment Tax Credit, subtract approximately one-third from these figures. A 6kW system nets out at $11,500–$14,700 for most homeowners.

Solar Cost by State (2026)

Costs vary by state due to labor markets, permitting complexity, and installer competition. Lowest cost states: Arizona ($2.50–$2.90/watt), Texas ($2.60–$3.10/watt), Florida ($2.65–$3.10/watt), North Carolina ($2.70–$3.20/watt). Mid-range states: Colorado ($2.80–$3.30/watt), Georgia ($2.85–$3.30/watt), Nevada ($2.75–$3.25/watt). Higher cost states: California ($3.20–$4.00/watt), New York ($3.30–$4.20/watt), Massachusetts ($3.10–$3.90/watt), Connecticut ($3.15–$3.85/watt). States with more competition among installers consistently come in at the lower end of these ranges.

What Drives the Cost of Solar Panels

Equipment costs (panels, inverter, racking) account for roughly 35–45% of a solar installation. Labor is 15–25%. Permitting, inspection, and interconnection fees are 5–10%. The installer's overhead and profit margin is 25–35%. This means the same physical equipment can cost significantly different amounts depending on which installer you use — justifying the time spent getting multiple quotes.

Cost After State and Local Incentives

The federal 30% ITC applies nationwide, but state incentives vary dramatically. Best stacked incentives: New York — federal 30% + state 25% credit (up to $5,000) + NYSERDA rebates. Massachusetts — federal 30% + state 15% credit (up to $1,000) + SMART program incentives. New Jersey — federal 30% + SREC income + no sales tax. New Mexico — federal 30% + state 10% credit (up to $6,000). Arizona — federal 30% + property tax exemption + no sales tax. States with only the federal credit: Texas, Florida, Colorado, Georgia — still a strong investment but lower total incentive stack.

How to Verify You're Getting a Fair Price

The simplest benchmark: divide the total quote by system size in watts. A fair per-watt price in 2026 is $2.50–$3.50 before incentives. Anything above $4.00/watt deserves scrutiny. Request itemized quotes that separate equipment from labor. Ask for the panel and inverter model numbers and look up their current market pricing — panels typically cost $0.30–$0.50/watt wholesale. Use SolarAtlas to see city-specific average savings and payback estimates before getting quotes, so you can evaluate whether a quote's projected ROI matches independent data.
